es.summary: Respuesta inmune inmediata tipo I provocada por la unión del IgE al alérgeno, con liberación de mediadores de mastocitos.
key_points: Mediada por anticuerpos IgE que se fijan a mastocitos y basófilos.
Desgranamiento de mastocitos libera histamina, leucotrienos y prostaglandinas.
Los síntomas aparecen en minutos y pueden progresar a anafilaxia.
El tratamiento incluye antihistamínicos, corticoides y epinefrina en casos graves.

pathophysiology: El alérgeno se une a IgE específico en la superficie de mastocitos y basófilos.
Esta unión desencadena la degranulación celular.
Se liberan mediadores como histamina, triptasa, leucotrienos y prostaglandinas.
Los mediadores provocan vasodilatación, aumento de la permeabilidad capilar y broncoconstricción.
risk_factors: Historia previa de reacciones alérgicas o anafilaxia.
Exposición frecuente a alérgenos (p.ej., picaduras de insectos, alimentos, medicamentos).
Atopia familiar (asma, rinitis alérgica, dermatitis atópica).
signs_symptoms: Hipotensión, taquicardia y sensación de desmayo.
diagnostics: Historia clínica y examen físico focalizado.
Niveles séricos de IgE total (IU/mL) y pruebas cutáneas de alergia.
Oxígeno arterial: PaO2 < 80 mmHg en casos graves.
Monitoreo de presión arterial y frecuencia cardíaca cada 5‑15 min durante la reacción.
treatment: Epinefrina IM 0.01 mg/kg (máx 0.5 mg) en anafilaxia.
Oxígeno suplementario y soporte de vía aérea si es necesario.
complications: Broncoespasmo severo que puede requerir ventilación mecánica.
Edema de vías aéreas superiores que compromete la respiración.
Daño renal secundario a hipotensión prolongada.
nursing_care: Evaluar signos vitales cada 5 min y registrar cambios.
Mantener vía aérea permeable; posicionar al paciente en decúbito supino con piernas elevadas si hay hipotensión.
Administrar medicamentos según orden y observar respuesta.
Preparar equipo de reanimación (epinefrina, oxígeno, vía IV).
patient_teaching: Llevar siempre una pulsera de alerta alérgica.
Uso correcto de autoinyectores de epinefrina y cuándo administrarlos.
Buscar atención médica inmediata ante síntomas de reacción sistémica.

outcomes: Sin caídas ni lesiones físicas durante la estancia hospitalaria
Paciente mantiene conciencia y orientado durante 24 h

interventions.action: Colocar al paciente en posición segura (decúbito supino con cabeza ligeramente elevada).
interventions.rationale: Reduce riesgo de aspiración y facilita la respiración.

interventions.action: Mantener el área de la cama libre de objetos que puedan causar tropiezos.
interventions.rationale: Previene caídas en caso de pérdida súbita de tono muscular.

interventions.action: Aplicar oxígeno por mascarilla facial si hay dificultad respiratoria.
interventions.rationale: Mejora la oxigenación y disminuye el riesgo de hipoxia cerebral.

interventions.action: Revisar y asegurar la vía IV y los dispositivos de monitoreo para evitar tirones.
interventions.rationale: Evita lesiones por desprendimiento accidental de catéteres.

interventions.action: Educar al paciente sobre la necesidad de reportar cualquier sensación de mareo o debilidad.
interventions.rationale: Promueve la autovigilancia y la prevención de lesiones.

en.summary: Immediate type I immune response triggered by IgE binding to allergen, releasing mast cell mediators.
key_points: Mediated by IgE antibodies that bind to mast cells and basophils.
Mast cell degranulation releases histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins.
Symptoms appear within minutes and may progress to anaphylaxis.
Treatment includes antihistamines, corticosteroids, and epinephrine in severe cases.

pathophysiology: Allergen binds specific IgE on mast cell and basophil surfaces.
Mediators such as histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins are released.
These mediators cause vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and bronchoconstriction.
risk_factors: History of prior allergic reactions or anaphylaxis.
Frequent exposure to allergens (e.g., insect stings, foods, medications).
Family atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis).
signs_symptoms: Hypotension, tachycardia, and feeling of fainting.
diagnostics: Focused medical history and physical exam.
Serum total IgE levels (IU/mL) and skin allergy tests.
Arterial oxygen: PaO2 < 80 mmHg in severe cases.
Monitor blood pressure and heart rate every 5‑15 min during reaction.
treatment: Epinephrine IM 0.01 mg/kg (max 0.5 mg) in anaphylaxis.
Supplemental oxygen and airway support if needed.
complications: Severe bronchospasm that may require mechanical ventilation.
Secondary renal damage from prolonged hypotension.
nursing_care: Assess vital signs every 5 min and record changes.
Maintain airway patency; position patient supine with legs elevated if hypotension present.
Administer medications per order and observe response.
Prepare resuscitation equipment (epinephrine, oxygen, IV access).
patient_teaching: Always wear an allergy alert bracelet.
Proper use of epinephrine auto‑injectors and when to use them.
Seek immediate medical care for systemic reaction symptoms.

outcomes: No falls or physical injuries during hospital stay
Patient remains alert and oriented for 24 h

interventions.action: Place patient in a safe position (supine with head slightly elevated).
interventions.rationale: Reduces aspiration risk and facilitates breathing.

interventions.action: Keep bed area free of objects that could cause tripping.
interventions.rationale: Prevents falls in case of sudden loss of muscle tone.

interventions.action: Administer oxygen via facial mask if respiratory difficulty.
interventions.rationale: Improves oxygenation and reduces risk of cerebral hypoxia.

interventions.action: Check and secure IV line and monitoring devices to avoid pulls.
interventions.rationale: Prevents injury from accidental catheter dislodgement.

interventions.action: Educate patient on reporting any dizziness or weakness.

summary.0.quote: IgE molecules bind together to an allergen and trigger mast cells to release chemical mediators like histamine, kinins, serotonin, slow-reacting anaphylaxis substances, and the neutrophil factor that produces allergic skin reactions, hay fever, and asthma.

key_points.0.quote: Sensitization The produced IgE antibodies attach to receptors on the surface of mast cells and basophils, which are types of immune cells found in tissues throughout the body.

key_points.1.quote: Release of chemical mediators The cross-linking of allergen with IgE antibodies on mast cells or basophils triggers the release of chemical mediators, including histamines, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins.

key_points.3.quote: Treatment for allergic reaction s may include antihistamines, steroids, and epinephrine.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: Allergen re-exposure If the sensitized individual is re-exposed to the same allergen, the allergen binds to the IgE antibodies on the surface of mast cells or basophils.

sections.pathophysiology.1.quote: The cross-linking of allergen with IgE antibodies on mast cells or basophils triggers the release of chemical mediators, including histamines, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins.

sections.pathophysiology.3.quote: This chemical mediator causes bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, and vasodilation.

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Common allergic responses are to seasonal allergens like various trees, ragweed, or pollens; medications; perennial allergens like dust or molds; latex ; animal dander; foods; household chemicals; fragrances; and insect stings or bites, as shown in Figure 24.2 .

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: The genetic tendency to develop allergic diseases such as allergic rhinitis , asthma, and atopic dermatitis is called atopy .

sections.risk_factors.3.quote: Indications for premedication may include patients with a history of an allergic reaction to blood transfusions, multiple transfusions, chronic illnesses, anxiety, febrile reaction s, or autoimmune disorders.

sections.diagnostics.1.quote: Diagnostic tests for hypersensitivity include complete blood count (CBC) with differential, eosinophil count, total serum IgE, and skin tests.

sections.diagnostics.3.quote: Obtain and document vital signs every hour for the duration of the transfusion.

sections.treatment.3.quote: Treatment for hemolytic transfusion reactions depends on the severity of the reaction and may include stopping the transfusion, frequently monitoring vital signs, administering IV fluids to maintain blood pressure, providing supplemental oxygen as needed, dialysis, management of bleeding, and supportive measures to manage the patient’s symptoms.

sections.complications.2.quote: Common symptoms of an allergic reaction include flushing, hives, rash, pruritus , difficulty breathing, laryngeal edema , wheezing, and possible anaphylaxis .

sections.complications.3.quote: Common symptoms of a hemolytic transfusion reaction include low back pain (first sign), chills, feeling of fullness, tachycardia, flushing, tachypnea , hypotension, bleeding, vascular collapse , and acute renal failure .

sections.nursing_care.0.quote: Obtain and document vital signs every hour for the duration of the transfusion.

sections.nursing_care.1.quote: Treatment for circulatory overload includes positioning the patient upright, lowering the feet in a dependent position, diuretics, oxygen, and bronchodilators.

sections.nursing_care.2.quote: Immediate interventions include discontinuing or removing the medication, managing the airway, administering oxygen as ordered, administering medications like epinephrine or diphenhydramine as ordered, and activating a rapid response in the event of anaphylaxis.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Some patients may be recommended to wear a medical alert bracelet to notify others of their allergies in the event of an emergency such as an extreme allergic reaction to peanuts, bee stings, or other allergens.
